title: Donations & the Ending
content_html:
Kathy the Carer: Competence and Complicity

By the time of the novel’s present, Kathy has been a carer for almost twelve years. She takes pride in her work: “My donors have always tended to do much better than expected. Their recovery times have been impressive.” Ishiguro makes Kathy’s competence deeply unsettling. Being a ‘good carer’ means helping donors survive long enough to give more organs. Kathy’s skill serves the very institution that will eventually kill her. Her pride in caring is both admirable and tragic — she cannot see that her competence makes her complicit.

Ishiguro never lets the reader forget this paradox. Kathy describes donors who “complete” after their second or third donation, their bodies failing from repeated organ removal. She uses the same calm, conversational tone for these deaths as she does for childhood memories. The reader must supply the horror that Kathy’s narration withholds. This is understatement as a narrative weapon: the quieter Kathy is, the louder the silence screams.

Key Fact

Kathy’s pride in being a good carer is the novel’s most subtle horror. Her skill helps donors survive long enough to give more organs — her competence makes her complicit in the system. Ishiguro shows how people can serve oppressive structures while believing they are doing good.

Ruth’s Confession

Ruth, now a donor whose body is failing, makes a deathbed confession to Kathy and Tommy. She admits she deliberately kept them apart because she was jealous of their connection: “I should have stepped back … I was the one who always wanted Tommy.” She gives them Madame’s address and urges them to apply for a deferral. Ruth’s confession is the novel’s most emotionally raw moment: she acknowledges her selfishness and tries to make amends before she “completes.”

Ruth’s confession is significant because it is the only moment in the novel where a character fully confronts their own wrongdoing. Ishiguro uses it to show that even within a dehumanising system, genuine moral reckoning is possible. Ruth’s regret does not undo the damage — Kathy and Tommy have lost years together — but it restores something: honesty. In a novel built on evasion and partial knowledge, Ruth’s directness is both brave and devastating.

Armed with Ruth’s information, Kathy and Tommy visit Madame and Miss Emily. They bring Tommy’s intricate animal drawings, hoping to prove their love and gain a deferral. Miss Emily’s response is devastating: “There is no deferral. There never has been.” The Gallery was not about judging love — it was about proving clones have souls. The entire deferral was a myth the clones created for themselves because the truth was unbearable.

Miss Emily also reveals the broader context. Hailsham was an experiment in humane treatment, but it failed: “How can you ask a world that has come to regard cancer as curable … to put away that cure?” Society did not want to know that clones were human. Hailsham has closed. The clones are now raised in conditions far worse. Ishiguro uses Miss Emily’s speech to show that good intentions alone cannot change a system built on exploitation.

Tommy’s Scream

After learning the deferral is a myth, Tommy asks Kathy to pull the car over. He gets out and screams. Kathy describes it with characteristic restraint: “His arms were stretched out on either side of him, his head was tilted back, and he was screaming.” The posture evokes a crucifixion. Tommy is, in this moment, a sacrificial figure — destroyed by a system he did not create and cannot fight.

But the scream passes. Tommy returns to the car, and they drive on in silence. This is the novel’s most devastating sequence: the one moment of genuine rebellion is brief, futile, and immediately followed by acceptance. Ishiguro’s point cuts deep — even when we briefly rage against mortality, we ultimately accept it. The scream is human; the silence that follows is also human.

Key Fact

Tommy’s scream is the novel’s only moment of raw protest. His crucifixion-like posture positions him as a sacrificial victim. But the protest passes instantly — he returns to quiet acceptance. Ishiguro shows that rebellion against mortality is real but brief; acceptance is the default human condition.

The Final Scene: Kathy at the Wire Fence

The novel closes with Kathy standing at a wire fence in Norfolk. Tommy has completed. Ruth is gone. Hailsham is closed. Kathy imagines everything she has lost blown towards her across the fields: “I keep thinking about this river somewhere, with the water moving really fast. And these two people in the water, trying to hold on to each other … But the current’s too strong.” Then she controls herself: “The fantasy never got beyond that — I didn’t let it.”

This self-correction is devastating. Kathy allows herself a moment of grief but pulls back before it overwhelms her. The phrase “I didn’t let it” captures the novel’s central tension: the gap between feeling and expression, between what the clones experience and what they permit themselves to acknowledge. The novel ends not with anger or despair but with quiet, devastating acceptance — and the reader is left to feel what Kathy cannot allow herself to feel.

Near the end, Kathy reflects: “What I’m not sure about is if our lives have been so different from the lives of the people we save.” This is the novel’s final provocation. Kathy suggests that ‘normal’ humans also live limited lives, also lose the people they love, also face mortality without being able to change it. The difference is one of degree, not kind. Ishiguro forces the reader to recognise themselves in the clones — to admit that the distance between ‘us’ and ‘them’ is smaller than we want to believe.
exam_tip_html: For part (a) on an ending extract, analyse Ishiguro’s sentence structures: short, controlled sentences show Kathy’s restraint, while the rare moments of longer, more emotional syntax reveal the feelings she is suppressing. For part (b), connect Tommy’s scream and Kathy’s “I didn’t let it” to the novel’s wider exploration of acceptance versus rebellion — strong AO4 material about how all humans manage the knowledge of mortality.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kathy’s competence as a carer makes her complicit in the system — her skill helps donors survive long enough to give more organs.
  • Tommy’s scream is the novel’s only moment of raw rebellion, but it passes immediately — acceptance is the default human condition.
  • The novel ends with Kathy controlling her grief (“I didn’t let it”), and her final reflection that the clones’ lives may not be “so different from the lives of the people we save.”

glossary_terms.definition: A clone who looks after other clones during their donation operations. Being a good carer means being complicit in the system that will eventually kill you.
A deliberate avoidance of dramatic expression, forcing the reader to supply the emotional response. A key feature of Ishiguro's writing style.
A rumoured postponement of donations, supposedly available to couples who prove they are truly in love. Miss Emily reveals it never existed.
The former head guardian of Hailsham who founded the school as an experiment in humane treatment of clones. She reveals the truth about the Gallery and the non-existence of deferrals.
An image of suffering and sacrifice with religious overtones. Tommy's pose with arms outstretched echoes the crucifixion, positioning him as a sacrificial victim.
The euphemistic term for a clone's death after their final organ donation. The word sanitises the reality of what is happening.
